question: What are the FIRST principles of good unit tests?
title: FIRST Principles Unit Tests | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.** Fast (milliseconds), Independent (no shared state), Repeatable (same result always), Self-validating (pass/fail automatically), Timely (written with the code). These principles ensure tests remain reliable and maintainable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have internalized testing principles beyond just writing tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the acronym or only knowing 2-3 of the 5 principles
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete violation example for each principle showing you understand the practical impact

sections.title: Five Properties of Good Tests
sections.content: **F**ast: unit tests should run in < 100ms — no database, no network, no file I/O. **I**ndependent: no shared state between tests, no ordering dependencies. **R**epeatable: same result on any machine at any time — no reliance on current time, random numbers, external systems. **S**elf-validating: test passes or fails automatically — no manual log inspection. **T**imely: written close to the code, ideally in TDD before the code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Fast: mock external deps; slow tests reduce feedback loop
- Independent: @BeforeEach resets state; no test-to-test dependencies
- Repeatable: avoid System.currentTimeMillis(), Random, network calls
- Self-validating: assertion must exist — assertEquals, not just System.out.println
- Timely: written with the code — tests written months later are harder and lower quality
- Violation example: flaky test that sometimes passes = not Repeatable
- Violation example: test order matters = not Independent

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: FIRST is the acronym for good unit test properties. Fast — unit tests should run in milliseconds by mocking external dependencies; slow tests mean developers stop running them. Independent — each test sets up its own state and can run in any order. Repeatable — same result every time on any machine, so no depending on the current time, random numbers, or network availability. Self-validating — the test clearly passes or fails with assertions, not print statements you inspect manually. And Timely — written close to the code, ideally before it in TDD. Violating any of these leads to tests that are unreliable, slow, or abandoned.

speakable_v2.standard_example: JUnit 5 tests for a Spring Boot service class with @Test and assertions
speakable_v2.hook: FIRST is the checklist that separates tests people trust from tests people work around.

beats.text: FIRST stands for Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely. It's a five-property checklist for good unit tests. Violate any one property and the test becomes unreliable, slow, or ignored.

Test suites decay over time if there's no standard. Slow tests kill developer feedback loops. Non-independent tests cause mysterious suite failures. FIRST gives a shared vocabulary for code reviews so bad tests get caught before they accumulate.

items: Fast: milliseconds — no real database, no network, no file I/O
Independent: no shared mutable state; any test can run in any order
Repeatable: same result on any machine at any time — no reliance on current time or randomness
Self-validating: clearly passes or fails via assertions — no manual log inspection
Timely: written close to the code, ideally before it in TDD

beats.text: A test that hits a real database violates Fast. A test that depends on the result of a previous test violates Independent. A test that calls LocalDate.now() without a Clock injection violates Repeatable — it'll behave differently depending on the date. production trap: non-Independent tests pass locally but fail in CI because CI parallelizes test execution differently, exposing the ordering dependency.

items: Tests that only print results without assertions — they always 'pass' (violates Self-validating)
Writing tests weeks after writing the code — they become much harder to get right and cover less (violates Timely)

speakable_v2.cap: FIRST isn't just theory — each property has a direct practical consequence when violated. Memorize it and you'll catch bad tests in code reviews.

question: Should you test private methods directly?
title: Testing Private Methods Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **No — test private methods through the public API.** Private methods are implementation details. If you feel the need to test a private method directly, it's a sign it should be refactored into its own class with a public method. Testing internals makes tests brittle — they break when you refactor without changing behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Testing philosophy — tests should test behavior, not implementation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using reflection to access private methods in tests — produces tests coupled to implementation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the refactoring signal: if a private method is complex enough to need its own tests, it belongs in its own class

sections.title: Test Behavior, Not Implementation
sections.content: Private methods support public methods — test them indirectly through the public API. If `calculateTaxBreakdown()` is private but called by `generateInvoice()`, testing `generateInvoice()` implicitly tests `calculateTaxBreakdown()`. **If a private method is so complex it needs its own tests**: extract it into a new class (`TaxCalculator`) with a public `calculateBreakdown()` method. Now it's testable and the refactoring is valid.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Don't use reflection to call private methods — brittle and wrong
- Private = implementation detail, not contract
- Test through public API that uses the private method
- Complex private method → extract to new class signal
- Tests that depend on internals break on safe refactors
- 'Test behavior not implementation' is the core principle
- Package-private is an alternative to private for testability (same package access)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I don't test private methods directly. Private methods are implementation details — the public API is the contract that should be tested. By testing through the public methods that call the private ones, I can refactor the internal implementation without breaking tests, as long as the public behavior is preserved. If a private method is so complex that I feel it needs its own test, that's a signal it should be extracted into its own class with a public method. Using reflection to call private methods is an antipattern — it couples tests to internals and makes them brittle.

question: What is the single responsibility principle for tests?
title: Single Responsibility in Tests | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Each test should verify one behavior — one reason to fail.** When a test fails, you should immediately know what broke. A test with multiple unrelated assertions across multiple methods is hard to diagnose. One concept per test doesn't mean one assertion — use assertAll for related properties of the same result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Test design principles — whether you write precise, focused tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a 'god test' that tests everything in one method — impossible to know which specific behavior broke
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between one concept per test (principle) and one assertion per test (too strict interpretation)

sections.title: One Reason to Fail
sections.content: A test should have **one logical concept** being verified — if it fails, you know immediately what broke. A test that checks: does the method save to DB AND send an email AND return the correct DTO — is testing three behaviors. If it fails, which behavior is wrong? Split into three focused tests. **Note**: multiple assertions on the same result are fine: `assertAll(() -> assertEquals(firstName,...), () -> assertEquals(lastName,...))` — these are one concept (the returned object is correct).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- One logical concept per test, not necessarily one assertion
- Multiple assertions on same result: use assertAll
- Multiple behaviors: split into separate test methods
- When it fails: test name + one assertion = immediate diagnosis
- 'God tests': test everything in one method — antipattern
- Test names guide: if you need 'and' in the name, split the test
- Exception: integration tests may reasonably test a full scenario

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Each test should verify one concept — one reason to fail. When a test fails in CI at 2am, I want the test name to tell me exactly what broke without needing to debug. If a test name has 'and' in it — like 'saves to database and sends email' — it's testing two things and should be split. That said, one concept doesn't mean one assertion: I can have multiple assertions with assertAll on the same return value — those are all verifying one concept, that the returned object is correct. The key question is: if this test fails, will I know immediately and precisely what broke?

question: How do you avoid flaky tests?
title: Avoid Flaky Tests Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Flaky tests pass sometimes and fail sometimes without code changes.** Common causes: relying on System.currentTimeMillis(), Thread.sleep(), shared mutable state, network calls, or random values. Fix by: injecting a Clock, using fixed test data, mocking external systems, and ensuring test independence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand test reliability and can diagnose common flakiness causes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Thread.sleep() to wait for async operations — race condition, not deterministic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give specific patterns: inject Clock for time, use Awaitility for async, mock random with fixed seed

sections.title: Root Causes and Fixes
sections.content: **Time dependence**: `System.currentTimeMillis()` / `LocalDate.now()` → inject `java.time.Clock` and use a fixed `Clock.fixed(instant, zone)` in tests. **Thread.sleep()**: used to wait for async — use Awaitility library instead (`await().atMost(2, SECONDS).until(() -> flag.get())`). **Shared state**: static fields or database state not reset between tests → @BeforeEach to reset, @Transactional to rollback. **External services**: mock them with Mockito or WireMock.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Inject Clock instead of System.currentTimeMillis()
- Use Awaitility for async test conditions — not Thread.sleep()
- @BeforeEach to reset shared state
- Mock external HTTP services: WireMock or MockWebServer
- Use @Transactional in Spring tests to auto-rollback DB changes
- Random values: inject Random with fixed seed or mock
- Test ordering dependency: @BeforeEach independent setup
- Environment differences: use Testcontainers for DB consistency

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Flaky tests fail intermittently without code changes — they erode trust in the test suite. The most common causes I've seen: time dependence where code calls LocalDate.now() directly — fix by injecting a Clock and providing a fixed clock in tests. Thread.sleep for async operations — this is a race condition, replace with Awaitility which polls until a condition is met or times out. Shared mutable state between tests — use @BeforeEach to reset. External network calls — mock with Mockito or WireMock. And test ordering dependencies — ensure @BeforeEach sets up everything the test needs independently.

speakable_v2.hook: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change is worse than useless — it erodes trust in your entire test suite.

beats.text: A flaky test passes sometimes and fails sometimes without any code change. Common causes: depending on the current time, using Thread.sleep for async operations, sharing mutable state between tests, relying on network calls, or depending on test execution order.

Flakiness erodes trust. When the build is 'probably fine', teams start ignoring failures. Bugs sneak through because nobody's sure if a red build is real or just flaky. Fixing flaky tests is high-leverage work.

items: Time dependence: LocalDate.now() gives different results on different days — inject Clock instead
Thread.sleep for async: a race condition, not a wait — use Awaitility to poll until a condition is met
Shared state: static mutable fields, database state not reset between tests — use @BeforeEach to reset
External network calls: mock them with Mockito or WireMock

beats.text: A membership expiry check that calls LocalDate.now() directly will pass on any day except the day someone set as the expiry date in test data. Fix: inject Clock, use Clock.fixed() in tests. production trap: Thread.sleep(500) for async is a race — on a slow CI server it won't be long enough and the test fails. Awaitility.await().atMost(2, SECONDS).until(() -> result.isDone()) is deterministic.

items: Increasing Thread.sleep duration to 'fix' a flaky async test — you're hiding a race condition, not fixing it
Ignoring flaky tests with 'it usually passes' — they accumulate and eventually block every build

speakable_v2.cap: Fix flaky tests immediately — each one left unfixed makes the next failure less credible and the suite less trustworthy.

question: How do you test time-dependent code in Java?
title: Testing Time-Dependent Code Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Inject `java.time.Clock` instead of calling `LocalDateTime.now()` directly.** In tests, provide `Clock.fixed(instant, zone)` to control the current time. This makes time-dependent logic testable without relying on the actual system clock.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical design for testability — a concrete example of 'design for testing'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling LocalDate.now() directly in business logic — untestable because the test can't control the current time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the actual pattern: constructor injection of Clock, use clock.instant() in code, Clock.fixed() in test

sections.title: Inject Clock, Control Time
sections.content: Production code: `class MembershipService { private final Clock clock; MembershipService(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; } boolean isExpired(Member m) { return m.expiresAt.isBefore(LocalDate.now(clock)); } }`. Production wiring: inject `Clock.systemDefaultZone()`. Test: `Clock testClock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2024-01-15T00:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC); MembershipService service = new MembershipService(testClock);` — now you fully control 'now'.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Avoid: LocalDate.now(), LocalDateTime.now() — not injectable
- Prefer: LocalDate.now(clock), LocalDateTime.now(clock)
- Inject Clock through constructor
- Test: Clock.fixed(instant, zone) — time never moves
- Production: Clock.systemDefaultZone()
- Pattern: design for testability = explicit dependencies
- Same principle: inject Random for testable random behavior
- Mockito alternative: mock the service method that returns time (less clean)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key is to inject Clock instead of calling now() directly. If business logic calls LocalDate.now() without a clock parameter, there's no way to control what 'now' is in a test. Instead, I declare a Clock field, inject it through the constructor, and call LocalDate.now(clock) in the business logic. In production I inject Clock.systemDefaultZone(). In tests I inject Clock.fixed with a specific instant — so the clock never moves and the test is fully deterministic. This is a general principle: make implicit dependencies like 'the current time' explicit through injection so tests can control them.

speakable_v2.standard_example: JUnit 5 tests for a Spring Boot service class with @Test and assertions
speakable_v2.hook: Calling LocalDate.now() directly in business logic makes your code untestable. The fix is two lines: inject a Clock, use now(clock).

beats.text: The pattern is simple: declare a Clock field, inject it through the constructor, and call LocalDate.now(clock) or LocalDateTime.now(clock) in business logic. In production, inject Clock.systemDefaultZone(). In tests, inject Clock.fixed(instant, zone) — a clock that never moves.

Code that calls LocalDate.now() directly has an implicit dependency on the real system clock. Tests can't control that dependency, so they can't reliably test date-sensitive logic — membership expiry, free trial periods, scheduling logic.

items: Production: inject Clock.systemDefaultZone() via Spring @Bean or constructor
Test: inject Clock.fixed(Instant.parse('2024-01-15T00:00:00Z'), ZoneOffset.UTC)
Usage: LocalDate.now(clock) — not LocalDate.now()

beats.text: MembershipService checks if a member's subscription is expired: return member.expiresAt.isBefore(LocalDate.now(clock)). In the test, you inject a fixed clock set to January 15th and set the expiry date to January 14th — the test deterministically validates expiry behavior. non-obvious: the same pattern works for any implicit dependency on the real world — inject Random with a fixed seed for testable random behavior, inject a UUID factory for testable ID generation.

items: Mocking the service method that returns the date rather than injecting Clock — less clean and couples tests to internals
Using LocalDate.now() in domain logic then patching it with static mocking — static mocking is a last resort; proper injection is the right solution

speakable_v2.cap: Clock injection is the textbook example of 'design for testability' — make implicit dependencies explicit so tests can control them.
